> I have a hierarchical space-time model investigating the interaction
> between county-level prescription opioid supply and socioeconomic
> conditions on drug overdose deaths. Reviewers would like to see the
> interaction results presented on the additive scale, which is the
> preferred way to present interaction results in epidemiology.
>
> Typically, I would do this by switching from the OR or RR to the
> average marginal effects by transforming back to the probability scale
> (rather than the log odds, for example) and aggregating (i.e.,
> marginalizing) the effect estimates on the probability scale. However,
> I have no idea how to do this from a complicated space-time model
> estimated in R-INLA.
>
> For this analysis, I fit a hierarchical model with Poisson
> distribution, using conditional autoregressive random effects to
> adjust for spatial autocorrelation, a vector of time-varying
> covariates, state fixed effects, and county random slopes, estimating
> the interaction using a two-way cross product term.
>
> Since I'm using restricted data for this analysis, I can't provide
> data, but I provide the code below (and if needed, I could simulate
> some data).
>
> #Make a copy of county number for county-level trend
> mydata14$ID <- cumsum(!duplicated(mydata14$COUNTY))
> countyTrend <- mydata14$ID
> y14 <- mydata14$drug_death
> e14 <- as.numeric(mydata14$POP) *
> sum(y14)/sum(as.numeric(mydata14$POP))
>
> #Create two-way cross-product term
> mydata14$PO_supply_X_Unemp <- mydata14$s.PO.supply *
> mydata14$s.UNEMPRATE
>
> formula.nbin <- y14 ~ 1 + f(ID, model = "bym", graph = Cnty3109.adj,
> constr = TRUE, scale.model = TRUE) +
>                             f(countyTrend, YearNum, model = "iid",
> constr = TRUE) +
>                             factor(mydata14$STATE) +
>                             factor(mydata14$YearNum) +
>                             factor(mydata14$RUCC) +
>                             s.pct.0_19 +
>                             s.pct.20_44 +
>                             s.pct.45_64 +
>                             s.pct.male +
>                             s.pct.nhwhite +
>                             s.pct.nhblack +

>                             s.pct.hs_less +
>                             s.pct.collegeplus +

messages.subject: Can INLA be used to fit non-linear fixed effect in LGCP?
messages.subject_clean: Can INLA be used to fit non-linear fixed effect in LGCP?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am fitting a LGCP using inlabru with some covariate information. However, the actual covariate relationship with the rate function is not log-linear. To be more concise, assume my covariate is X, my current model has the following form:

eta = g(X; alpha) + U,

Here g is a non-linear function of X and alpha is the parameter vector determining the structure of g. U is the spatial random effect.

I am wondering if INLA can be used to fit such a model which would also provide me with inference on the non-linear parameter alpha. If so, how can I implement this in INLA?

Thank you very much!
David

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can INLA be used to fit non-linear fixed effect in LGCP?
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

there are two types of linearity here; whether the relationship between covariate and eta is nonlinear in the covariate, and whether the eta is nonlinear in the latent Gaussian variables. It’s not entirely clear which kind of nonlinearity you’re referring to.
Nonlinearity in the latent variables can be handled in inlabru (and is one of the reasons inlabru exists) Nonlinearity in the covariate effect in the sense of e.g. a rw2 model where the covariate is the domain can be handled in both. For constructing the lgcp likelihood, inlabru is usually the easiest alternative.

If the nonlinearity is with respect to the latent variables, you can implement it in inlabru using an R expression that calls the needed nonlinear function that computes the contribution to eta. The tricky part here is the it needs to be constructed so inlabru itself can evaluate it at new locations. The details of this depends on your precise model definition.

 For things like an rw2 model of a spatial covariate, see the online covariate examples for inlabru for some syntax options.

Depending on the details on your model structure, there may be specific tricks, so I can’t say much more without a more complete mathematical model definition for the desired predictor.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can INLA be used to fit non-linear fixed effect in LGCP?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can INLA be used to fit non-linear fixed effect in LGCP?
messages.body_plain:
Ok!

For regular georeferenced observations, that would be as simple as defining alpha as some suitable transformation alpha_fun() of a N(0,1) variable, and writing the predictor formula as X^alpha_fun(alpha_component)

For lgcp models, it’s a bit harder. The alpha part would work exactly the same, but the X-evaluation becomes the harder part. (X*beta)^alpha would be easier, if you already know the sign of the effect, since then you can define X*beta as a regular linear effect of the covariate, and inlabru knows how to spatially evaluate those. But for the model as you wrote it, you have (at least) two options:
1. Define a function that evaluates the spatial covariate at the input locations and call that function in the predictor formula, or
2. Define a linear predictor component for X, but set the latent mean to 1 and the precision to a large value.

The kind of function needed for X in alternative 1. Is the same type as function used in some of the covariate examples for inlabru (there is an bru_fill_missing() function that fills missing values with the nearest available value, which is usually preferable to the fill_with_zero used in the old examples.)

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can INLA be used to fit non-linear fixed effect in LGCP?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can INLA be used to fit non-linear fixed effect in LGCP?
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

since the predictor expression in inlabru in principle can be any R expression, it's difficult to cover all possible models in the examples, especially those that are essentially current research problems (in terms of how well the iterative method and the resulting posterior approximation behaves, etc).
But with your additional details, here's how one can do it in your case:

alpha_fun can be used to specify a specific prior distribution, yes. Since you say alpha is known to be strictly positive, that just means you need a strictly possible transformation there.
For example, say you want an exponential distribution for alpha. Then qexp(pnorm(u),rate=...) has an exponential distribution with given rate parameter, if u is N(0,1). Replace qexp() with the quantile function for whatever prior distribution you want for alpha.
Below I'll assume X is a SpatialGridDataFrame where the first data column is the covariate.

alpha_fun <- function(u) {
  qexp(pnorm(u), rate=prior_rate)
}
comp <- ~ - 1 + Xbeta(X, model = "linear") +
   alpha_internal(1, model="linear", mean.linear=0, prec.linear=1) +
   U(coordinates, model=spde)
form <- coordinates ~ abs(Xbeta)^alpha_fun(alpha_internal) + U

The model above defines eta = |X*beta|^alpha + U. The absolute value is just there to guard against X*beta becoming negative, which would break when alpha becomes a non-integer.
In order for the iterative method to work, you need to initialise the beta coefficient (so the derivatives aren't zero in the first iteration):

fit <- bru(components = comp, like(model="cp", data=..., samplers=...), options=list(bru_initial=list(Xbeta=1)))

Note:  The alpha_fun definition can be made more numerically robust by using branching for pos/neg u, and log.p and lower.tail arguments to qexp and pnorm. I plan to add automated helpers for this to inlabru soon, since it's such a common thing to want to do.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
In principle I think one can also do the X^alpha*beta + U version of the model, by using that model="offset" in inlabru can be used to evaluate constants:

comp <- ~ - 1 + x(X, model = "offset") + beta(1, model="linear") +

   alpha_internal(1, model="linear", mean.linear=0, prec.linear=1) +
   U(coordinates, model=spde)

form <- coordinates ~ beta * x^alpha_fun(alpha_internal) + U

This "offset" feature should really be called "const", and may be renamed to that in the future; the name "offset" is just because it was initially just the internal implementation of offset() in inlabru.
I haven't used this feature myself yet, so please let me know if you try it, and if it works or not! (it is tested by the package tests, but those can't cover all use cases).

(Also note I didn't include an intercept parameter in the code examples; add that in if you need one...)

Finn

On Sun, 1 Aug 2021 at 21:51, Finn Lindgren <finn.l...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi David,
>
> since the predictor expression in inlabru in principle can be any R expression, it's difficult to cover all possible models in the examples, especially those that are essentially current research problems (in terms of how well the iterative method and the resulting posterior approximation behaves, etc).
> But with your additional details, here's how one can do it in your case:
>
> alpha_fun can be used to specify a specific prior distribution, yes. Since you say alpha is known to be strictly positive, that just means you need a strictly possible transformation there.
> For example, say you want an exponential distribution for alpha. Then qexp(pnorm(u),rate=...) has an exponential distribution with given rate parameter, if u is N(0,1). Replace qexp() with the quantile function for whatever prior distribution you want for alpha.
> Below I'll assume X is a SpatialGridDataFrame where the first data column is the covariate.
>
> alpha_fun <- function(u) {
>   qexp(pnorm(u), rate=prior_rate)
> }
> comp <- ~ - 1 + Xbeta(X, model = "linear") +
>    alpha_internal(1, model="linear", mean.linear=0, prec.linear=1) +
>    U(coordinates, model=spde)
> form <- coordinates ~ abs(Xbeta)^alpha_fun(alpha_internal) + U
>
> The model above defines eta = |X*beta|^alpha + U. The absolute value is just there to guard against X*beta becoming negative, which would break when alpha becomes a non-integer.
> In order for the iterative method to work, you need to initialise the beta coefficient (so the derivatives aren't zero in the first iteration):
>
> fit <- bru(components = comp, like(model="cp", data=..., samplers=...), options=list(bru_initial=list(Xbeta=1)))

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the two quotes are really saying the same thing. In the second quote, imagine that the "unconsidered effect" that the covariates did not account for is due to elevation; that's what the first quote is describing, that if the other covariates can't describe effect due to elevation, and elevation isn't included in the model, then the spatial model component is likely to pick that information up instead.

In practice, it's not usually as simple as that, since each model component can really only be interpreted in relation to the other components. For example, if elevation _is_ included as a linear effect in the model, as well as a general spatial component, but the actual elevation effect is non-linear, then the non-linear part of the effect is likely to be picked up by the spatial component. Also, there will be some indeterminacy in what the spatial field picks up and what the explicit elevation component picks up, since if it wasn't for the prior distributions, the components would not be completely identifiable from real data.  Therefore, in some models, the choice of prior distributions can be very important. So check that you've set all the prior distributions according to your problem. "Default priors" can be extremely problematic when the model is prior-sensitive.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Can INLA be used to fit non-linear fixed effect in LGCP?
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Can INLA be used to fit non-linear fixed effect in LGCP?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, that's correct.
The alpha_internal-->alpha transformation can be seen as a 1-dimensional copula transformation; In the prior, alpha_internal is N(0,1) and alpha has the distribution determined by the chosen quantile function. In the posterior, alpha_internal has some posterior distribution, and alpha has the distribution obtained when feeding that distribution through the quantile(pnorm()) transformation.  The inla.tmarginal() function from INLA can be used to calculate the posterior density for alpha. Alternatively, use the predict() method to estimate the posterior summary statistics using posterior sampling.

Here's the theory for it:
P(alpha <= a) = P(alpha_fun(u) <= a) = P(quantile_fun(pnorm(u)) <= a)
  = P(pnorm(u) <= cdf_fun(a)) = P(u <= qnorm(cdf_fun(a)))
where cdf_fun is the CDF function for the prior model for alpha and u is alpha_internal.

INLA has functions for computing the transformation from alpha_internal: Using inla.tmarginal(alpha_fun, marginal) should produce the posterior density for alpha itself, when given the marginal density output for alpha_internal.
Or inla.emarginal(alpha_fun, marginal) for just the posterior expectation.

Finn

> > >    U(coordinates, model=spde)

> > >

> > > > But with your additional details, here's how one can do it in your case:
> > > >
> > > > alpha_fun can be used to specify a specific prior distribution, yes. Since you say alpha is known to be strictly positive, that just means you need a strictly possible transformation there.
> > > > For example, say you want an exponential distribution for alpha. Then qexp(pnorm(u),rate=...) has an exponential distribution with given rate parameter, if u is N(0,1). Replace qexp() with the quantile function for whatever prior distribution you want for alpha.
> > > > Below I'll assume X is a SpatialGridDataFrame where the first data column is the covariate.
> > > >
> > > > alpha_fun <- function(u) {
> > > >   qexp(pnorm(u), rate=prior_rate)
> > > > }
> > > > comp <- ~ - 1 + Xbeta(X, model = "linear") +
> > > >    alpha_internal(1, model="linear", mean.linear=0, prec.linear=1) +

messages.subject: How to estimate Probability of Incidence greater 1 per 10000 population
messages.subject_clean: How to estimate Probability of Incidence greater 1 per 10000 population
messages.body_plain:
Hi
all,

I am fitting a spatio-temporal
interaction model with negative binomial likelihood using r-INLA with Leroux
prior for space and Rw1 for time. I have included environmental covariates
(Xit, i=1,2,...s; t=1,2,....t) as fixed effects and ‘O’ the observed case counts
as dependent variable in the model. The negative binomial mean is
parameterized as,

Mean = r * E,

where ‘r’ is the relative risk and

E is the expected incidence = ratio
of observed ‘O’ in a month in an area to cumulative no. of cases for all the
months in a year * population of the area.

 I have used the following r-script
for fitting the model:

f <- O ~ X1 + X2 + X3 + X4 + X5 + X6 + X7 + X8 +

                f(ID.area,

model="besag",

graph=Qs,

constr=TRUE,

rankdef=1,

hyper=list(prec=list(prior=sdunif))) +

  f(ID.month,

                    model="rw1",

   constr=TRUE,

  rankdef=1,

  hyper=list(prec=list(prior=sdunif)))
+

   f(ID.area.month,

                    model="generic0",

                    Cmatrix=R,

                    rankdef=r.def,

   hyper=list(prec=list(prior=sdunif)),

    constr=TRUE,

    extraconstr=list(A=Bst,
e=rep(0,nrow(Bst))))

Model <- inla(f,

                family
= "nbinomial",

                  data
= data,

                  E=E,

                 control.fixed=
list(prec.intercept = 1, prec=1),

                 control.inla
= list(tolerance=1e-6, strategy =strategy, int.strategy = "eb",
cmin=0),

                 control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,
waic=TRUE, cpo = TRUE, config = TRUE),

                 control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE,
cdf=c(log(1))),

                  verbose
= TRUE)

Having fitted the model, I understand that the
function “cdf=clog(1)” estimates the exceedance probability for relative risk
>1. However, I am interested to know the areas in which probability of incidence
> 1 per 10,000 populations. I would appreciate if anyone can help me
calculating the Prob(incidence >1 per 10000 populations)?

Thank you very much!

Uma maheswari.R

messages.body_plain:
I guess if you know the ``expected'' population size you can do that.

' > 1'  is 1-(Prob(0) + Prob(1))

so if you know the posterior for the linear predictor, you can simulate
from that one to estimate Prob(0) and Prob(1), and then you have it as
above.

the '10000' corresponds to the scaling 'E', as you have to adjust E
depending on this, like setting E=10000, when you estimate the
probabilities above. (if your 'E' is in ``number of people'' or similar)

Try this out with Poisson data first and a simple model.

messages.subject: Issues with predictions using INLA on HPC with CentOS7
messages.subject_clean: Issues with predictions using INLA on HPC with CentOS7
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I am using INLA to estimate the effects of climate on disease risk. I have a very large sent (over 100K observations) and so I am running the model in an HPC. I am running the model multiple times leaving one year out at the time (leave-one-year-out cross-validation). One major issue I am facing is that the predictions for some years are extremely higher than those for the other years (i.e. 15 orders of magnitude or more). The issue here is that these extreme predictions do not occur always in the same year or in the same location which leads me to believe that this is either caused by a misspecification of the model or a problem with CentOS7. Any pointers would be appreciated. I must mention that when I run the models in my laptop (macOS) the results are sensible. Unfortunately, due to the computational cost of the runs, I cannot make all runs in the laptop.

The priors and the model equation are below.

hyper.bym <- list(prec.unstruct=list(prior='pc.prec',param=c(1, 0.01)),
                  prec.spatial=list(prior='pc.prec', param=c(1, 0.01)))
hyper.ar1 <- list(prec=list(prior='pc.prec',param=c(3, 0.01)),
                  rho=list(prior='pc.cor1', param=c(0.5, 0.8)))
hyper.iid <- list(prec=list(prior='pc.prec',param=c(3, 0.01)))
hyper.rw1 <- list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.01)))

f0 <- total ~ 1 +
   f(ID.area, model='bym',
     graph=sea.adj,
     constr=TRUE,
     scale.model=TRUE,
     hyper=hyper.bym) +
   f(ID.month, model='rw1',
     hyper = hyper.rw1,
     group=ID.country,
     control.group = list(model='iid',
                          hyper=hyper.iid)) +
   f(ID.year, model="iid", hyper=hyper.iid) +
   f(inla.group(tas02, n=10, method="quantile"),
     model="rw1", hyper=hyper.rw1) +
   f(inla.group(dry02, n=10, method="quantile"),
     model="rw1", hyper=hyper.rw1) +
   urban +
   gdp2 +
   log(flux_rad) +
   log(total_arrivals)

model0 <- inla(as.formula(f0),
                     family="nbinomial",
                     data=train_set,
                     offset=log(population),
                     control.fixed=list(prec=1,prec.intercept=1),
                     control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=1),
                     control.compute=list(config=FALSE, dic=FALSE),
                     control.inla=list(strategy="gaussian",
                                       int.strategy="eb",
                                       h=0.3),
                     verbose=FALSE)

Best,
Felipe

messages.body_plain:
Hi Haavard,

Do you need my data & files? Here is the code that I have been running;

#my data files
meanRes2 <- readRDS(paste(dir, "/data/dat.res.RDS", sep = "")) %>%
    filter(timePeriod %in% c("0.5")) %>%
  droplevels()

meanRes2 <- meanRes2 %>%
   mutate(tagID = as.factor(tagID),
        tagID2 = as.numeric(tagID2),
        recv = as.factor(recv),
        recv2 = as.factor(recv2),
        rSite = as.factor(rSite),
        session = as.numeric(season),
        session = as.factor(session),
        sexAge = as.factor(sexAge),
        date = as.factor(date)) %>%
  select(tagID, tagID2, rSite, sexAge, season, session, recv,recv2, yday, durationMins) %>%
   mutate(sex = as.character(sexAge),
         life_stage = case_when(sex %in% c("F", "M") ~ "Adult",
                                sex %in% c("J") ~ "Juvenile",
                                TRUE ~ sex),
         life_stage = as.factor(life_stage)) %>%
  group_by(tagID, tagID2, rSite, life_stage, season, session,  recv, recv2, yday) %>%
  summarise(meanRes = mean(durationMins)) %>%
  select(tagID, tagID2, rSite, life_stage, season, session, recv, recv2, yday, meanRes) %>%
  distinct() %>%
  as.data.frame()

meanRes2$rSite <- recode(meanRes2$rSite, "Site A" = "site_A", "Site B" = "site_B")

#PC Prior

sd <- sd(meanRes2$meanRes)
U <- 3 * sd(meanRes2$meanRes)
priorpc <- list(prec = list(prior = "pc.prec", param = c(U, 0.05)))

# 1. Create a grid of covariate values

MyData <- ddply(meanRes2,
              .(session, rSite, recv2, life_stage))

#B. Create X matrix with expand.grid
Xmat <- model.matrix(~ session + rSite + recv + life_stage, data = MyData)
head(Xmat)
Xmat <- as.data.frame(Xmat)

# 3. Run the model in INLA with the inla.make.lincombs option
lcb <- inla.make.lincombs(Xmat)

I5.Pred <- inla(meanRes ~ session + f(yday, model = "ar1", hyper = priorpc, replicate= tagID2) + f(tagID, model = "iid", hyper = priorpc),
                lincomb = lcb,                                     #predicted values stuff
                control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE),
                control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
                quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975),
                family = "gamma",
                control.family = list(hyper = Hyper.Gam),
                data = meanRes2,
                verbose=TRUE)

Does that help? If not I will send my data files/code.

Thanks, I appreciate your help!

Brittany

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Name for Gaussian observation component?
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

The prediction “formula” is a general R expression with access to the latent model components and hyperparameters, so one way to include observation randomness in predictions is to add a call to rnorm(). So something like this should do what you want:

~ Intercept + site + rnorm(numberofpredictionlocations, sd=1/sqrt(Precision_for_the_Gaussian_observations))

(Note that you have to use the explicit name for the intercept component, and not just +1, as that would literally just add the constant 1 to the expression)

Finn

you might have data so that removing a year makes a big difference.

r.full = inla(...)

			control.mode=list(result=r.full, restart=TRUE))

}

let me know if there are still issues

H

messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have property price data at the individual house level (N=146786) which is grouped by post code zones (J=1784). There are two types of explanatory variables in the data set: the first at the property level (lower-level) and the second at the post code level (upper-level). The response is the log value of each house.

I am exploring the BYM2 model to account for the spatial structure as a random intercept at the upper-level in a multilevel model. The spatial structure is defined using the 6 k-nearest neighbours (of the post codes) represented in a symmetric binary weight matrix (W). The lower-level observations are indexed by an integer to the respective row-position in the weight matrix W (code attached).

I fitted two models, one including all lower-level and upper-level covariates (inla_mres) and a second ignoring the explanatory variables at the upper-level (inla_mres2). In the results, the precision of the random effects at the upper-level decreased from 50 to 20 (which is somehow in line with the expectation). However, the mixing parameter (phi value) is lower than 0.1 in both models, 0.046 and 0.064, respectively. I interpret these as if the spatial structure was virtually null and the random effects were almost completely iid, which would not make sense since property prices display high spatial autocorrelation. Am I doing something wrong in my code or is it matter of interpretation given my data and the precision parameter?

Please see the summary of the models below and find the code attached.

Any help or clarification would be very much appreciated!
Rafa

Could not attached R code. But you can see it here:

# Organize data -----------------------------------------------------------

set.seed(3)
library(Matrix)
library(data.table)
library(tidyverse)
library(INLA)
library(spdep)

# Temporal stages
stages <-
  c("stage_before_2010", "stage_2010_2012",  "stage_2012_2013",   "stage_2013_2015",
    "stage_2015_2016", "stage_2016_2018", "stage_2018_2019")
# Read property data
values <- readRDS('output/temp/rq1_valuesreduced.rds')
# Subset only one of the temporal stages in the data
values_s <- values[stage == stages[1]]
rm(values)
# Order value by postcode id
values_s <- values_s[order(values_s$codpost_id),]
values_s$fcodpost_id <- factor(values_s$codpost_id)
values_s <- droplevels(values_s)
# Index individual observations by position in M
values_s$codpost_inla <- as.integer(values_s$fcodpost_id)

# Extract postcode level weight matrix
# Post code w centroids
od_points <- read_csv('data/od_points/points_postcodes.csv')
od_points <- od_points[order(od_points$GEOID),]
# Filter post codes with data
od_points_s <- od_points[od_points$GEOID %in% values_s$codpost_id,]
od_points_s <- od_points_s[order(od_points_s$GEOID),]
# Compute k nearest nb at post code level
pc_coords <- as.matrix(od_points_s[,c('X','Y')])
# Create matrix
knn <- 6
knearnb_pc <- knn2nb(knearneigh(pc_coords, knn, longlat = TRUE), row.names = od_points_s$GEOID)
knearnb_pc <- make.sym.nb(knearnb_pc)
W <- as(nb2mat(knearnb_pc, style = 'B'), 'Matrix')

# Model -------------------------------------------------------------------

# Model specifications
inla_model <- 'bym2'

# BYM2 prior
# References:
# Rieble et al., 2016
# https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/0962280216660421
bym2_prior <- list(
  prec = list(
    prior = "pc.prec",
    param = c(.2/0.31, 0.01)),
  phi = list(
    prior = "pc",
    param = c(0.5, 0.5))
)

# Model 1 -----------------------------------------------------------------

# Define formula
model_form <- log_value ~ log_size + cveclase + bathrooms_cat + parking_cat + log_age + age_2 +
  year_val + nom_ent +
  education_bi + public_administration_bi + inv_arboles_dispone + inv_alumpub_no_dispone + park_bi + crime_homicidios +
  log_hh_car +  access_car_opt + access_nlm4
# Read base formula
form_inla <- update(model_form, . ~ . + f(codpost_inla, model=inla_model, graph=W, hyper = bym2_prior, scale.model = TRUE, constr = TRUE))
# Fit model
inla_mres <- inla(form_inla, family = 'gaussian', data=values_s, control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE))

# Model 2 -----------------------------------------------------------------

# Define formula
model_form2 <- log_value ~ log_size + cveclase + bathrooms_cat + parking_cat + log_age + age_2 +
  year_val + nom_ent
# Read base formula
form_inla2 <- update(model_form2, . ~ . + f(codpost_inla, model=inla_model, graph=W, hyper = bym2_prior, scale.model = TRUE, constr = TRUE))
# Fit model
inla_mres2 <- inla(form_inla2, family = 'gaussian', data=values_s, control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE))

# Results -----------------------------------------------------------------

summary(inla_mres)
summary(inla_mres2)

‘nb2mat’ will take an ‘nb’ object and create an adjacency matrix that INLA can take. ‘listw2mat’ will create a weight matrix from a list object. Also, you can convert these matrices into sparse matrices with as(matrix, “Matrix”), for example.

Best,

Virgilio

read shape file ##us.poly<-readShapePoly(system.file("cb_2016_us_county_500k.shp", package="spdep")) us.poly<-readOGR("cb_2016_us_county_500k.shp") # Remove Alaska(2), Hawaii(15), Puerto Rico (72), Guam (66), Virgin Islands (78), American Samoa (60) # Mariana Islands (69), Micronesia (64), Marshall Islands (68), Palau (70), Minor Islands (74) #us.poly <- us.poly[!us.poly$STATEFP %in% c("02", "15", "72", "66", "78", "60", "69", # "64", "68", "70", "74"),] # Make sure other outling islands are removed. #us.poly <- us.poly[!us.poly$STATEFP %in% c("81", "84", "86", "87", "89", "71", "76", # "95", "79"),] # create inla weight matrices list.queen<-poly2nb(us.poly, queen=TRUE) cards<-card(list.queen) tr<- which(cards==0) # Merge spatial df with downloade ddata. sub.poly<- us.poly[-tr,] leafmap2 <- merge(sub.poly, county_dat, by=c("GEOID"), all=FALSE) list.queen2<-poly2nb(leafmap2, queen=TRUE) set.ZeroPolicyOption(TRUE) W<-nb2listw(list.queen2, style="W", zero.policy=TRUE) #W1<-nb2mat(list.queen2, style="W", zero.policy=TRUE) WW<-listw2mat(W) W2<-as(WW, "Matrix") # graph data popup_dat2 <- paste0("County: ", leafmap2$NAME, "
Value: ", leafmap2$airqlty) pal2 <- colorQuantile("YlOrRd", NULL, n = 20) leaflet(data = leafmap2) %>% addTiles() %>% addPolygons(fillColor = ~pal(airqlty), fillOpacity = 0.8, color = "#BDBDC3", weight = 1, popup = popup_dat2) plot(W, coordinates(leafmap2)) ## INLA library(INLA) # setup data D <- data.frame(leafmap2) leafdata<-transform(D, GEOID = as.numeric(GEOID)) leafdata <- leafdata[ , c("GEOID", "airqlty")] ID<-seq(1:NROW(leafdata)) leafdata <- cbind(leafdata, ID) E <-rep(100, NROW(leafdata)) formula <- airqlty ~ 1 + f(ID, model="bym", graph = W2, hyper = list(prec.unstruct = list(prior="loggamma", param=c(1,0.01)), prec.spatial = list(prior="loggamma", param=c(1,0.001 )))) mod<-inla(formula, family="poisson", E=E, data=leafdata, verbose=TRUE)

messages.body_plain:
With a logit link you would restrict the probabilities to lie between 0 and 1 inclusive - not so with a log link which is why prior restrictions are needed.

You can, through sampling, obtain RR's from logit models. See:

Rose, Charles E., Yi Pan, and Andrew L. Baughman. 2015. “Bayesian Logistic Regression Modeling as a Flexible Alternative for Estimating Adjusted Risk Ratios in Studies with Common Outcomes.” Journal of Biometrics & Biostatistics 6 (4): 1–32. https://doi.org/10.4172/2155-6180.1000253.
John

messages.body_plain:
using a log link then you lose control that prob < 1, as the log() link
only make sense for small probabilities, but then its essentailly is the
same as logit link. Personally, I do not see any good justification for
using the log link in this setting.

there is an intermediate link, 'loga', which you can use, see attached,
and you can run this in a sequence of a to use the previous fit as an
initial value in the next one , ending up with a=close to zero which is
the log link.

messages.body_plain:
I would guess that the spatial information is essentially there in the
covariates, hence the 'excess' information, after you have adjusted for
the covariates is not that much.

of course, there is a confounding between the effect of the covariates
and the spatial term, but I guess here the covariates are so strong that
this effect essentially goes away.

Best
H

messages.subject: Survival fit with Gompertz distribution is not plausible
messages.subject_clean: Survival fit with Gompertz distribution is not plausible
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA-group,

I try to fit treatment-data for teeth to a survival model. When using the package "flexsurv" with a Gompertz distribution the fit followes nicely the original data. However, when I repeat the fit with INLA, the fit looks different. Right now I cannot decide whether I use INLA in a wrong way or the INLA-fit is wrong because of the "experimental" status of the Gompertz-distribution. The survival-analysis with INLA follows the instructions from the book "Bayesian inference with INLA" from Virgilio Gómez-Rubio.

Here is a reproducible example:

library(survival)
library(flexsurv)
library(INLA)
library(parallel)
library(ggplot2)

# create random data
# parameters from the initial flexsurf fit on original data
#      shape       rate
# -0.2290890 -0.7998633

random_data<-data.frame(time = rgompertz(n = 1e3,
                                         shape = -0.2290890,
                                         rate = exp(-0.7998633)),
                        cens = 1)
# In my original data set, I have data for eight years. To adjust for this
# time-span all times longer than eight years will be censored
random_data[random_data$time > 8, 'time']<-8
random_data[random_data$time == 8, 'cens']<-0

# Kaplan-Meier plot of the random data
km<-survfit(Surv(time,cens)~1,
            data=random_data)
plot(km)

# fit with flexsurv
flexsurv_model<-flexsurvreg(Surv(time,cens) ~ 1,
                            data = random_data,
                            dist = 'gompertz')
plot(flexsurv_model)
coef(flexsurv_model)
#      shape       rate
# -0.2391953 -0.7735919
# visual fit and recovered parameters are very close to the original data

# fit with INLA
sinla <- inla.surv(random_data$time, random_data$cens)
inla_model <- inla(sinla ~ 1,
                   data = random_data,
                   family = "gompertzsurv")
summary(inla_model)
# the recovered parameters look different from the original ones

# plot fit
# Grid of times
time <- seq(0.01, 8, by = 0.1)
# Marginal of alpha
alpha.marg <- inla_model$marginals.fixed[["(Intercept)"]]
# Set number of cores to use
options(mc.cores = 4)
# Compute post. marg. of survival function
surv.inla <- mclapply(times, function(t){
  surv.marg <- inla.tmarginal(function(x) {exp(- exp(x) * t)}, alpha.marg)
  surv.stats <- inla.zmarginal(surv.marg, silent = TRUE)
  return(unlist(surv.stats[c("quant0.025", "mean", "quant0.975")]))
})

surv.inla <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, surv.inla))
surv.inla$times<-times

km_data<-data.frame(time=km$time,
                    surv=km$surv,
                    lb=km$lower,
                    ub=km$upper)
ggplot(km_data,aes(x=time))+
  geom_line(aes(y=surv))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lb,ymax=ub),alpha=0.3)+
  geom_ribbon(data=surv.inla, aes(ymin=quant0.025,ymax=quant0.975),alpha=0.3)+
  geom_line(data=surv.inla, aes(y=mean))

                                         rate = exp(-1.355)),

                    surv=km2$surv,
                    lb=km2$lower,
                    ub=km2$upper)

  geom_line(aes(y=surv))+
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lb,ymax=ub),alpha=0.3)+
  geom_ribbon(data=surv.inla, aes(ymin=quant0.025,ymax=quant0.975),alpha=0.3)+
  geom_line(data=surv.inla, aes(y=mean))

# there is a nice fit of the inla-fit with the new random-data

> > > nicely the original data. However, when I repeat the fit with
> > > INLA,

> > INLA
> > > in a wrong way or the INLA-fit is wrong because of the
> > "experimental"
> > > status of the Gompertz-distribution. The survival-analysis with
> > > INLA
> > > follows the instructions from the book "Bayesian inference with
> > INLA"
> > > from Virgilio Gómez-Rubio.
> > >
> > > Here is a reproducible example:
> > >
> > > library(survival)
> > > library(flexsurv)
> > > library(INLA)
> > > library(parallel)
> > > library(ggplot2)
> > >
> > > # create random data
> > > # parameters from the initial flexsurf fit on original data
> > > #      shape       rate
> > > # -0.2290890 -0.7998633
> > >
> > > random_data<-data.frame(time = rgompertz(n = 1e3,
> > >                                          shape = -0.2290890,
> > >                                          rate = exp(-0.7998633)),
> > >                         cens = 1)
> > > # In my original data set, I have data for eight years. To adjust
> > for
> > > this
> > > # time-span all times longer than eight years will be censored

> > > random_data[random_data$time == 8, 'cens']<-0
> > >
> > > # Kaplan-Meier plot of the random data
> > > km<-survfit(Surv(time,cens)~1,
> > >             data=random_data)
> > > plot(km)
> > >
> > > # fit with flexsurv
> > > flexsurv_model<-flexsurvreg(Surv(time,cens) ~ 1,
> > >                             data = random_data,
> > >                             dist = 'gompertz')
> > > plot(flexsurv_model)
> > > coef(flexsurv_model)
> > > #      shape       rate
> > > # -0.2391953 -0.7735919
> > > # visual fit and recovered parameters are very close to the
> > > original
> > > data
> > >
> > > # fit with INLA
> > > sinla <- inla.surv(random_data$time, random_data$cens)
> > > inla_model <- inla(sinla ~ 1,
> > >                    data = random_data,
> > >                    family = "gompertzsurv")
> > > summary(inla_model)
> > > # the recovered parameters look different from the original ones
> > >
> > > # plot fit
> > > # Grid of times
> > > time <- seq(0.01, 8, by = 0.1)
> > > # Marginal of alpha
> > > alpha.marg <- inla_model$marginals.fixed[["(Intercept)"]]
> > > # Set number of cores to use
> > > options(mc.cores = 4)
> > > # Compute post. marg. of survival function
> > > surv.inla <- mclapply(times, function(t){
> > >   surv.marg <- inla.tmarginal(function(x) {exp(- exp(x) * t)},
> > > alpha.marg)
> > >   surv.stats <- inla.zmarginal(surv.marg, silent = TRUE)
> > >   return(unlist(surv.stats[c("quant0.025", "mean",
> > > "quant0.975")]))
> > > })
> > >
> > > surv.inla <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, surv.inla))
> > > surv.inla$times<-times
> > >
> > >
> > > km_data<-data.frame(time=km$time,
> > >                     surv=km$surv,
> > >                     lb=km$lower,
> > >                     ub=km$upper)
> > > ggplot(km_data,aes(x=time))+
> > >   geom_line(aes(y=surv))+
> > >   geom_ribbon(aes(ymin=lb,ymax=ub),alpha=0.3)+
> > >   geom_ribbon(data=surv.inla,
> > > aes(ymin=quant0.025,ymax=quant0.975),alpha=0.3)+
> > >   geom_line(data=surv.inla, aes(y=mean))
> > > # the plot also looks different from the original data
> > >
> > > # crosscheck with new data according to the recovered parameters
> > >
> > > random_data2<-data.frame(time = rgompertz(n = 1e3,

> > >                                          rate = exp(-1.355)),

> > > # In my original data set, I have data for eight years. To adjust
> > for
> > > this
> > > # time-span all times longer than eight years will be censored
> > > random_data2[random_data2$time > 8, 'time']<-8
> > > random_data2[random_data2$time == 8, 'cens']<-0
> > >
> > > # Kaplan-Meier plot of the random data

Dear Havard,

Many thanks for the advise. Yes, that sorted all my issues.

Felipe

On Thursday, August 5, 2021 at 6:57:19 AM UTC+1 he...@r-inla.org wrote:
>
> I do not think this a centOS7 issue.
>
> you might have data so that removing a year makes a big difference.
>
> to make it more stable (or to check), please do a full run and then use
> that as the initial value for each year removal. something like this
>
> r.full = inla(...)
>
> for(year in ...) {
>
> data[year] <= NA
>
> r[[year]] <- inla(...,
> control.mode=list(result=r.full, restart=TRUE))
>
> }
>
>
> let me know if there are still issues
>
> H
>
>
> On Mon, 2021-08-02 at 05:48 -0700, 'felipe...@googlemail.com' via R-inla
> discussion group wrote:
> > Hello,
> >
> > I am using INLA to estimate the effects of climate on disease risk. I
> > have a very large sent (over 100K observations) and so I am running
> > the model in an HPC. I am running the model multiple times leaving one
> > year out at the time (leave-one-year-out cross-validation). One major
> > issue I am facing is that the predictions for some years are extremely
> > higher than those for the other years (i.e. 15 orders of magnitude or
> > more). The issue here is that these extreme predictions do not occur
> > always in the same year or in the same location which leads me to
> > believe that this is either caused by a misspecification of the model
> > or a problem with CentOS7. Any pointers would be appreciated. I must
> > mention that when I run the models in my laptop (macOS) the results
> > are sensible. Unfortunately, due to the computational cost of the
> > runs, I cannot make all runs in the laptop.
> >
> > The priors and the model equation are below.
> >
> > hyper.bym <- list(prec.unstruct=list(prior='pc.prec',param=c(1,
> > 0.01)),
> >                   prec.spatial=list(prior='pc.prec', param=c(1,
> > 0.01)))
> > hyper.ar1 <- list(prec=list(prior='pc.prec',param=c(3, 0.01)),
> >                   rho=list(prior='pc.cor1', param=c(0.5, 0.8)))
> > hyper.iid <- list(prec=list(prior='pc.prec',param=c(3, 0.01)))
> > hyper.rw1 <- list(theta = list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(1,0.01)))
> >
> > f0 <- total ~ 1 +
> >    f(ID.area, model='bym',
> >      graph=sea.adj,
> >      constr=TRUE,
> >      scale.model=TRUE,
> >      hyper=hyper.bym) +
> >    f(ID.month, model='rw1',
> >      hyper = hyper.rw1,
> >      group=ID.country,
> >      control.group = list(model='iid',
> >                           hyper=hyper.iid)) +
> >    f(ID.year, model="iid", hyper=hyper.iid) +
> >    f(inla.group(tas02, n=10, method="quantile"),
> >      model="rw1", hyper=hyper.rw1) +
> >    f(inla.group(dry02, n=10, method="quantile"),
> >      model="rw1", hyper=hyper.rw1) +
> >    urban +
> >    gdp2 +
> >    log(flux_rad) +
> >    log(total_arrivals)
> >
> > model0 <- inla(as.formula(f0),
> >                      family="nbinomial",
> >                      data=train_set,
> >                      offset=log(population),
> >                      control.fixed=list(prec=1,prec.intercept=1),
> >                      control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE, link=1),
> >                      control.compute=list(config=FALSE, dic=FALSE),
> >                      control.inla=list(strategy="gaussian",
> >                                        int.strategy="eb",
> >                                        h=0.3),
> >                      verbose=FALSE)
> >
> > Best,
> > Felipe

messages.body_plain:
Hi Finn,

Thanks so much for the clarification. We were just using the default priors, so I will look into adding prior distributions.

- Kristin

On Sunday, August 1, 2021 at 5:43:46 PM UTC-4 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi,
>
> the two quotes are really saying the same thing. In the second quote, imagine that the "unconsidered effect" that the covariates did not account for is due to elevation; that's what the first quote is describing, that if the other covariates can't describe effect due to elevation, and elevation isn't included in the model, then the spatial model component is likely to pick that information up instead.
>
> In practice, it's not usually as simple as that, since each model component can really only be interpreted in relation to the other components. For example, if elevation _is_ included as a linear effect in the model, as well as a general spatial component, but the actual elevation effect is non-linear, then the non-linear part of the effect is likely to be picked up by the spatial component. Also, there will be some indeterminacy in what the spatial field picks up and what the explicit elevation component picks up, since if it wasn't for the prior distributions, the components would not be completely identifiable from real data.  Therefore, in some models, the choice of prior distributions can be very important. So check that you've set all the prior distributions according to your problem. "Default priors" can be extremely problematic when the model is prior-sensitive.
>
> Finn
>
> On Sat, 31 Jul 2021 at 05:08, KB <kjb...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > After reading some tutorials and published literature using R-INLA, I am really confused about what the Gaussian random field (GRF) of the SPDE models represents. It is unclear to me whether the Gaussian random field represents the spatial variability of the response variable with or without covariates. When I ran an SPDE model with covariates and with the intercept only, the Gaussian random field maps looked identical for both models. Does this mean that the Gaussian random field represents the spatial variability of the response variable without the covariates?
> >
> > We would like to produce a map of the expected values of the model given by exponential(covariates) x exponential(spatial random field). How can I produce this spatial map using an R-INLA SPDE negative binomial model?
> >
> > Below are a few references I found in regards to explaining the GRF, which I found confusing.
> > 1) The following source says that the "GRF represents the variation of the response variable in space, once all of the covariates are accounted for and that examining the spatial distribution of the GRF could reveal which covariates are missing. For example, if elevation is positively correlated with the response variable, but is not included in the model, we could see a higher posterior mean in areas with higher elevation"
> > (https://ourcodingclub.github.io/tutorials/spatial-modelling-inla/)
> >
> > 2) However, in the following articles, the authors indicate the spatial random fields represents the data without the covariates.
> >
> > "The spatial effect map created with INLA-SPDE represents the intrinsic spatial variability of the data after excluding environmental variables. Therefore, when the pattern of the spatial map is similar to the map of the prediction, it implies there is an unconsidered effect that is driving the majority of the observed spatial distribution."
> > (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-020-73879-3)
> >
> > "The spatial component represents the intrinsic spatial variability of the data without variables." (Pennino, M. Grazia, et al. "Bayesian spatio-temporal discard model in a demersal trawl fishery." Journal of Sea Research 90 (2014): 44-53).
> >

> using a log link then you lose control that prob < 1, as the log() link
> only make sense for small probabilities, but then its essentailly is the
> same as logit link. Personally, I do not see any good justification for

>
> there is an intermediate link, 'loga', which you can use, see attached,

Hi  Håvard,

Many thanks for your help.

There is a quite strange behavior across INLA versions. The results that I mentioned earlier occurr when I run the code in INLA version 21.2.23. Here the full

messages.body_plain:
I would guess its a data/model miss-match and it there are issues
locating the mode of the hyperparameters.

Often inaccuracies can be fixed doing a rerun

	r = inla(...)
	r = inla.rerun(r)

Can you upgrade to R-4.1 and install the most recent testing version and
rerun? with that version, try also adding

	r = inla(..., inla.mode="experimental")

Otherwise, I would need code & data to rerun it here

Best
H

messages.body_plain:
The possibility of negative shapes would be great! When analyzing tooth data and the data follows a Gompertz-distribution, the shape is always negative.
In the following example you can see the time to the first intervention per person. The black line is the Kaplan-Meier-curve, the red line is the fit with a Gompertz-distribution (flexsurv). The dataset contains 7e6 observations:

he...@r-inla.org schrieb am Freitag, 6. August 2021 um 18:02:29 UTC+2:
>
> I'll have to check what implications this might have
>
> On Fri, 2021-08-06 at 03:58 -0700, Heinz-Werner Priess wrote:
> > This sounds like a plausible reason. Using shape > 0 for random-data I
> > have no problems to recover my parameters in the INLA-fit.
> > However, my original data follows a Gompertz-distribution with
> > negative shape. Is there any possibility to allow negative shapes in
> > the INLA-fit?
> >
> > he...@r-inla.org schrieb am Freitag, 6. August 2021 um 12:50:16 UTC+2:
> > >
> > > you simulate with shape = -0.229... and the INLA implementation
> > > assumes
> > > shape > 0, so this can be the reason.
> > >

> > > > surv.inla$time<-times
> > > > to make the the plot possible.
> > > >
> > > > However, I the parameters I get from the INLA-fit deviate from the
> > > > parameters of the initial distribution. The result is essentially
> > > the
> > > > same as my first fit.

> > > > Initial Distribution:

> > > >                                          shape = -0.2290890,
> > > >                                          rate = exp(-0.7998633)),

> > > >
> > > > > summary(inla_model)

> > > > Model hyperparameters:

> > > > Posterior marginals for the linear predictor and
> > > >  the fitted values are computed

> > > >                          cens = 1)
> > > > shape = 0.001 is not the same as shape = -0.229

> > > >
> > > > inappropriate_fit.png

> > > > > there were some errors in the code, please try now

> > > > > >
> > > > > > I try to fit treatment-data for teeth to a survival model.

> > > > > using
> > > > > > the package "flexsurv" with a Gompertz distribution the fit
> > > > > > followes
> > > > > > nicely the original data. However, when I repeat the fit with
> > > > > > INLA,
> > > > > > the fit looks different. Right now I cannot decide whether I
> > > > > > use
> > > > > INLA
> > > > > > in a wrong way or the INLA-fit is wrong because of the
> > > > > "experimental"
> > > > > > status of the Gompertz-distribution. The survival-analysis
> > > > > > with
> > > > > > INLA
> > > > > > follows the instructions from the book "Bayesian inference
> > > > > > with
> > > > > INLA"
> > > > > > from Virgilio Gómez-Rubio.
> > > > > >
> > > > > > Here is a reproducible example:

> > > > > > library(survival)
> > > > > > library(flexsurv)
> > > > > > library(INLA)
> > > > > > library(parallel)

> > > > > >

> > > > > >                                          shape = -0.2290890,
> > > > > >                                          rate = exp(-
> > > 0.7998633)),
> > > > > >                         cens = 1)
> > > > > > # In my original data set, I have data for eight years. To
> > > adjust
> > > > > for
> > > > > > this
> > > > > > # time-span all times longer than eight years will be censored
> > > > > > random_data[random_data$time > 8, 'time']<-8
> > > > > > random_data[random_data$time == 8, 'cens']<-0
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # Kaplan-Meier plot of the random data
> > > > > > km<-survfit(Surv(time,cens)~1,
> > > > > >             data=random_data)
> > > > > > plot(km)
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # fit with flexsurv
> > > > > > flexsurv_model<-flexsurvreg(Surv(time,cens) ~ 1,
> > > > > >                             data = random_data,
> > > > > >                             dist = 'gompertz')
> > > > > > plot(flexsurv_model)
> > > > > > coef(flexsurv_model)
> > > > > > #      shape       rate
> > > > > > # -0.2391953 -0.7735919
> > > > > > # visual fit and recovered parameters are very close to the
> > > > > > original
> > > > > > data
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # fit with INLA
> > > > > > sinla <- inla.surv(random_data$time, random_data$cens)
> > > > > > inla_model <- inla(sinla ~ 1,
> > > > > >                    data = random_data,
> > > > > >                    family = "gompertzsurv")
> > > > > > summary(inla_model)
> > > > > > # the recovered parameters look different from the original
> > > > > > ones
> > > > > >
> > > > > > # plot fit
> > > > > > # Grid of times
> > > > > > time <- seq(0.01, 8, by = 0.1)
> > > > > > # Marginal of alpha
> > > > > > alpha.marg <- inla_model$marginals.fixed[["(Intercept)"]]
> > > > > > # Set number of cores to use
> > > > > > options(mc.cores = 4)
> > > > > > # Compute post. marg. of survival function
> > > > > > surv.inla <- mclapply(times, function(t){
> > > > > >   surv.marg <- inla.tmarginal(function(x) {exp(- exp(x) * t)},
> > > > > > alpha.marg)
> > > > > >   surv.stats <- inla.zmarginal(surv.marg, silent = TRUE)
> > > > > >   return(unlist(surv.stats[c("quant0.025", "mean",
> > > > > > "quant0.975")]))
> > > > > > })
> > > > > >
> > > > > > surv.inla <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, surv.inla))
> > > > > > surv.inla$times<-times
> > > > > >
> > > > > >

> > > > > >                     surv=km$surv,

> > > > > > ggplot(km_data,aes(x=time))+
> > > > > >   geom_line(aes(y=surv))+

messages.subject: Question about categorial fixed effect interpretation
messages.subject_clean: Question about categorial fixed effect interpretation
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have been running some basic models to understand the effect of specifying a manual intercept with data stacks on an SPDE model. The test model I'm running has no random effects, only the fixed effect of a binary factor variable. When I run this model with an automatic intercept: inla(culex_tarsalis_females ~ trap_type, data=abun2, family="poisson"), the mean for the intercept and second level of the coefficient make sense and have reasonable SDs. When I run the same model with a manual intercept to mimic the data stack for SPDE: inla(culex_tarsalis_females ~ -1 + Intercept + trap_type, data=abun2, family="poisson"), where Intercept is a vector of 1's, there is an fixed intercept where I'm guessing the interpretation is meaningless in the absence of one of the binary factor categories. I can see how the intercept is derived, but I'm not sure how the coefficient for the second level of the factor is calculated. Also, for the manual intercept model, the SDs are identical and huge. I can reduce the SDs by specifying a large prior precision on the fixed effects, but that changes the fixed coefficients as well and I worry about generalizability and "data hacking" in that case.

My questions are 1) why are the SDs so much larger for the model where I manually specify the intercept (this was the case in my more complicated SPDE model as well) and 2) what is the best approach to getting reasonable estimates? Alternatively, is there a better way to deal with factor variables in a data stack that may resolve some of these issues?

Sorry for the long-winded explanation here. I appreciate any guidance you have with this!

Best,
Pascale

messages.body_plain:
When using an explicit intercept covariate, the automated factor handling for removing the first level to get contrasts doesn’t work. (That’s also the likely problem you had when having an SPDE model involved)  You wither need to use the full factor and no intercept, or include an intercept but manually convert the factor variable to a set of indicator variables, to ensure identifiability. You can use model.matrix separately on the factor to help with the conversion.

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

the group features defines a kronecker precision between the "main" model and the group model ("separable covariance" usually refers to a kronecker product covariance, which is the same as having a kronecker product precision), so you may still be able to use that.
However, the invariance structure of the kronecker product of two intrinsic stationary models is messy, so a lot of problems tend to occur for such models.  For single models, the invariance is usually handled by a constraint. For the kronecker product that's less easy.  There's been some discussion about this in recent weeks/months.  But I'm not sure if that's the problem you encounter, or if there's a problem with your code.

If the two dimensions are two dimensions of space, it's usually much more sensible two use a 2D-lattice GMRF instead; the common 4-neighbour ICAR model only has one invariant vector (the constant field).
INLA has the rw2d model, which is a smoother 2D ICAR model.
If you're building a model for two covariates, then a kronecker product model can make more sense, but anytime you use intrinsic models you have to know how to deal with the invariances.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] How to interpret the threshold of excursion sets for the spatial random effect from LGCP
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] How to interpret the threshold of excursion sets for the spatial random effect from LGCP
messages.body_plain:
Hi David,

[Beware, long answer!]

there are a few different ways LGCP models are used, and the practical interpretation differs a bit between them,
and it may help to understand that aspect first.
It turns out that it's not really the intractability of the exact posterior distribution that's the issue, but rather more fundamental aspects of the models, and interpretation of excursion sets in general.
Below, I've tried to give a "brief" introduction to both the LGCP interpretation itself, and to what excursion sets of posterior distributions really mean.

A: The original LGCP construction was made to get a (weakly) clustered point process model;
With u(s) being a Gaussian random field, define the function lambda(s)=exp(u(s)).
Conditionally on u(), we can then define Y as an inhomogeneous Poisson point process with intensity function lambda(s).
The resulting distribution for Y, integrating out u(), is not a Poisson point process, but rather a more clustered process.
If we repeat this for i=1,...,M, we get both a new latent processes u_i and new point patterns Y_i.
There is limited information about each u_i, but with more and more realisations of Y_i we can get more information about the fixed covariance parameters for the u_i processes.

B: But what if we took just a single realisation of u(), but multiple realisations Y_i of the point pattern model, _conditionally_ on that fixed u()?
Then we would in principle get more and more information about u itself with more realisations Y_i.
This isn't what the LGCP construction initially was intended for, but is instead a different hierarchical model, where u is a fixed but unknown log-intensity field.

In practice, what often happens is that we only have a single realisation of the point pattern Y_i available.
In this situation, the data itself cannot distinguish between the two separate model structures A and B defined above;
both model structures are applicable, and mathematically we cannot distinguish them.
Only knowledge of the problem will tell us which interpretation is the most appropriate one.

Computing excursion sets for lambda (or equivalently, for u) essentially implicitly assumes that we are in situation B; we view lambda as a fixed unknown function over space, and we want to know where it is large.

So if we want to know where lambda is above a certain threshold T, we seek locations such that P(lambda(s) > T | Y) is large, which is the same as P(u(s) > log(T) | Y).
(I'll just deal with pointwise probabilities here; with the "excursions" package one can also find sets with given _joint_ probability.)

A common thing to do is to go straight to the _posterior_mean_ of u(), and threshold it.
For easier theory, let's switch to the posterior _median_, and call it m(s), defined via P(u(s) <= m(s) | Y) = 0.5,
and also P(u(s) > m(s) | Y) = 0.5

The excursion set E of a threshold log(T) of m(s) is then points where m(s) > log(T)
For all s in E,
0.5 = P(u(s) > m(s) | Y)
  = P(u(s) - log(T) > m(s) - log(T) | Y)
  <= P(u(s) - log(T) > 0 | Y)
  = P(u(s) > log(T) | Y)

So for points in E, where m(s) > log(T), the probability P(u(s) > log(T) | Y) is greater than or equal to 0.5.
The set E can also be seen as the _largest set_ such that  P(u(s) > log(T) | Y) >= 0.5, so in this particular case,
the excursion set of the posterior median of the intensity field (or log-intensity) field has a clear probabilistic meaning in relation
to the unknown true intensity field.

With the methods developed for the "excursions" package, this can be generalised to construct "credible regions" for excursions of lambda(s) (via u(s)) with control of the joint excursion probabilities,
but it's important to remember that excursions of m(s) are not the same thing as excursions of u(s); it's just a _point_estimate_ of the true excursions.

Note, that nowhere above did the tractability or intractability of the likelihood and distributions come into the discussion!
That's merely a question for how accurately the relevant posterior probabilities can be calculated. Due to the relative non-informativeness of point pattern data in this context, the posterior distribution of u(s) is usually very well approximated by a Gaussian random field (given that the prior is Gaussian as well), so the posterior distribution calculations in INLA are quite good.

The fundamentals of interpreting the model itself, and the interpretation of posterior properties of the random field is instead the crucial step for understanding the excursion set question, and this is where there is a lot of confusion.
Traditionally, this was mostly ignored, and point estimates like excursions of m(s) were taken as corresponding directly to excursions of u(s).  It gets even more complex when one starts also to consider excursions of multiple levels of u(s) at the same time (like for contour maps), and point estimates other than the median, such as quantile fields (for example to get a set where the probability for u(s) to exceed log(T) is 95%, either individually or jointly).

We discuss some aspects of the excursion set interpretation in three papers, both by Bolin and Lindgren:
https://rss.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/rssb.12055
https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2016.1228537
https://www.jstatsoft.org/article/view/v086i05

PS. I am not aware of all this being properly discussed in any courses anywhere, so you're not alone in being confused about this!
I hope the above introduction to the more rigorous interpretation of posterior excursion sets is helpful!

Best wishes
Finn

> Hi all,
>
> My question is not really about INLA but more about the theoretical understanding of LGCP. But I guess I may have the best chance of getting some help here.
>
> If I understand the structure of LGCP correctly, the posterior distribution of the spatial random effect of a LGCP should be analytically intractable. Unlike the standard kriging where the posterior is still a Gaussian process, an analytically intractable posterior distribution means that we don't really have a very good way of interpreting some of the distributional structure of the posterior spatial random effect.
>
> This makes me confused about how to interpret the threshold value for calculating excursion sets. For example, if the posterior is still a Gaussian process, then we may be able to interpret the excursion threshold value as something like how many standard deviation above the mean. However, if the posterior distribution is no longer a Gaussian process, this interpretation no longer seems to make sense.
>
> I guess to make my question more concrete, what I am wondering about specifically is that if I set a certain threshold value, say 0.5, what exactly does this threshold value represent with respect to the spatial random effect? Thank you very much!
>
> David

Hi Finn,

Thanks so much for the detailed explanation. But I guess my original question was not clear about what I was exactly confused about. My main problem is that in some situations (my current situation), the threshold T is not pre-specified. Unlike in some cases, for example, where people are interested in regions of high CO2 level, people may pre-determine the threshold T to be say 300 PPM. This choice of T to be 300 PPM has clear physical and environmental reasons. However, in my current situation, I do not have a pre-specified T, so if I set my T = 0.5, what does this T = 0.5 mean? I looked at a paper by Peter Diggle from 2005 where they suggested to use the quantile of log-normal distribution to principally construct the threshold. But my main issue with that is if the posterior of the latent process u(s) is no longer a Gaussian process, why would we use the quantile of log-normal distribution? But from what you said, it seems that we are only approximating the posterior of u(s) by a Gaussian process, so we can get away with that. Is this the way to understand this?

Thanks,
David

Hi,
When there isn’t a pre-specified threshold, one needs to ask oneself what the purpose of finding an excursion set _at all_ is. When the question is clear, one can then figure out how to find the answer. Presumably, the paper you mentioned had a specific goal in mind. Other goals would lead to other thresholds.

As for lognormal vs normal vs exact posterior, this again depends on the goal. Specifically, _which_ lognormal distribution did they take a quantile from?
The quantiles of the posterior distribution for lambda varies over space, so I’m guessing that they used a quantile from the estimated _model_ distribution for lambda, I.e. the marginal distribution one would have if the estimated model was exact, and modeling framework A from my previous reply was the relevant one, where each new realisation would generate a new u() (and lambda()) process?
But that still leaves the question of what the goal of constructing an excursion set is.

Finn

messages.subject: Precision matrix using kappa and tau
messages.subject_clean: Precision matrix using kappa and tau
messages.body_plain:
Hi there,

I'm working with some simulated data and I would like to get the Precision matrix using kappa and tau. I have seen that we can do it using rho and sigma but not with kappa and tau. I tried with this example for a gaussian response: y = f(si) + epsilon, but I'm not completely sure. If you can help me I will be grateful.

# INLA code
inla.seed = sample.int <http://sample.int>(n=1E6, size=1)

sim_loc = matrix(c(0,0,3,3, 0, 3, 3, 0), nrow = 4, byrow = T)
mesh_sim = inla.mesh.2d(loc = sim_loc, max.edge=c(0.5, 1))
plot(mesh_sim)
mesh_sim$n

spde = inla.spde2.matern(mesh_sim, alpha = 2)

Q = inla.spde.precision(spde, theta=c(exp(spde$param.inla$theta.initial[1]), exp(spde$param.inla$theta.initial[2])))
omega_s = inla.qsample(n=1, Q = Q, seed = inla.seed)
omega_s = omega_s[ ,1]  # Spatial random field

# Simulated data
n = 1000
loc = matrix(runif(2*n), n)*10 # coordinates

A = inla.spde.make.A(mesh=mesh_sim, loc=loc)
omega_s = drop(A %*% omega_s)

# Linear predictor
beta0 <- 1
sigma_e <- 0.5
lin.pred <- beta0 + omega_s

# Response variable
y <- lin.pred + sigma_e*rnorm(n)

Thanks!!

messages.subject: Phylogenetic comparative analysis with INLA
messages.subject_clean: Phylogenetic comparative analysis with INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm currently trying to replicate the following MCMCglmm model using INLA, but without success so far. The objective is to estimate the coefficients of effects of 'fixed effect' predictors on the response while controlling for non-independence among data points (species) due to their evolutionary relationships ('phylogeny'). According to a Brownian motion model, which I'm assuming, the covariance among data points (species) drops linearly and proportionally with increasing distance in evolutionary time.

A phylogeny in this case is an ultrametric bifurcating representation of evolutionary distances in time ('branch lengths') among species, with tips (the individual species) connected by internal nodes (which also connect to each other via other nodes), and a root node connecting everything. Branch lengths vary among each pair of connecting nodes and tips, but all tips are the same distance from the root.

#############################################
#Example MCMCglmm analysis setup on a simulated dataset#
#############################################

library(MCMCglmm);
data(bird.families);#This is a representation of the phylogenetic relationships among bird families (although I refer to 'species' elsewhere, in this example it's families)#

#Simulate some data
set.seed(123456)
phylo.effect<-MCMCglmm::rbv(bird.families, 1, nodes="TIPS")#"Random Generation of MVN Breeding Values and Phylogenetic Effects". "TIPS" are the families - we don't have trait values for internal nodes. The '1' here refers to the variance of the simulated values#

set.seed(23456)
phenotype<-phylo.effect+rnorm(dim(phylo.effect)[1], 0, 1)#Adding the non-phylogenetic component of trait variation#

test.data<-data.frame(phenotype=phenotype, taxon=row.names(phenotype))

#Create a sparse inverse matrix of the phylogeny#
 Ainv<-MCMCglmm::inverseA(bird.families)$Ainv#This includes all tips (species) and internal nodes (for the latter we have no trait data)#

#Run the analysis#
prior<-list(R=list(V=1, nu=0.002), G=list(G1=list(V=1, nu=0.002)));

model<-MCMCglmm(phenotype~1, random=~taxon, ginverse=list(taxon=Ainv), data=test.data, prior=prior);

This estimates the intercept and the phylogenetic and residual variance components. The estimate and uncertainty of the intercept in this model are modified due to the non-zero phylogenetic random effect for bird families.

I've tried several INLA model setups to replicate this, but without success. These include copying the animalINLA model setup, with either model="generic0" or model="generic2", and with the inverse matrix for the bird families input using Cmatrix (including only tips, but created by subsetting the Ainv object above to just tips, rather than inverting the matrix based on tips alone; according to MCMCglmm documentation this would seem to be okay). Here's the model:

inla(phenotype~f(spN, model="generic2", hyper = list(theta1 = list(param = c(0.5, 0.5), fixed = FALSE),theta2 = list(param = c(0.5, 0.5), fixed = FALSE)), constr = TRUE, Cmatrix = AinvSM) + 1,data=testdata,control.family = list(hyper = list(theta = list(initial = 10, fixed = TRUE))));

I'm totally guessing here, but I wonder if INLA is assuming that the bird families are equidistant in evolutionary time? I used numeric 1:N families as rownames in Cmatrix, and made an equivalent numeric variable in the data table (spN) to cross reference with it. But if INLA is assuming equidistance, what is the purpose of the Cmatrix?

I compared MCMCglmm with INLA (using the animalINLA setup with "generic2" as above) for the intercept and phylogeny random effect using 100 datasets simulated as above. I found that the intercept means were at least proportional (with r^2=0.5) but with much narrower credible intervals in INLA, almost exclusively non-overlapping with the true population value. For the phylogenetic random effect, there is a relationship between the MCMCglmm and INLA estimates (r^2~0.2) but it's more noisy and not proportional (slope~0.5).

If I've done something completely wrong please let me know!

I see there have been related questions previously, but so far I don't have the impression there's a conclusive answer.

Many thanks for your time!

All the best, Richard.

messages.body_plain:
Richard,

You must not subset your precision matrix (Ainv)! Doing this destroys the model structure, since precision matrix is indicating conditional model structure. You can subset covariance matrix (this indicates marginal model structure) and invert it if you want, but given that we can setup the phylogenetic precision matrix directly I see no point in doing this.

Gregor

Thanks!

Ben

Finn

messages.body_plain:
Richard,

I advise against subsetting the covariance matrix and inverting it compared to building the inverse (precision) matrix directly. Why? Because inversion with floating point introduces some error. Best to go directly with the precision matrix you can build form the phylogeny directly. Furthermore, you could be interested in the inferred value of "internal" nodes in your downstream analysis (after model fitting). Also, subsetting covariance matrix and inverting it is in essence still estimating all the nodes, but not directly - the removed nodes become part of your model with more involved precision matrix between the sample nodes (tips) - precision matrix of the subset will be denser and indicate the relationships between your samples nodes (tips) due to removed internal nodes.

I will not comment on the priors - I suggest you look at each model documentation (in PDF), which describe model parameterisation and default priors, which you can control with functions such as control.family() and others!

gg

messages.body_plain:
Thanks Gregor, ultimately I'll run it as you advise, once I'm sure I'm correctly cross-referencing the full inverse matrix with the data table. As a side note, in the ?MCMCglmm documentation under the option 'nodes' it says: "...For phylogenies "TIPS" estimates effects for the tips only, and for pedigrees a vector of ids can be passed to nodes specifying the subset of individuals for which animal effects are estimated. Note that all analyses are equivalent if omitted nodes have missing data but by absorbing these nodes the chain max mix better. However, the algorithm may be less numerically stable and may iterate slower, especially for large phylogenies." I guessed from this that subsetting the full inverse matrix would give the same result given that internal nodes have no data, but I may have misinterpreted.

However, I still think there could be an issue with the setup of the INLA analysis. After some changes to the model I presented before, I'm now getting good estimates of the phylogenetic random effect, BUT including the phylogenetic random effect in the model decreases uncertainty in the 'fixed effect' model relative to excluding it, whereas it should increase uncertainty due to statistical non-independence (as happens when running the MCMCglmm model I presented). I think the INLA model may be interpreting the phylogenetic random effect as an additional 'phylogenetic noise' component on top of the linear fixed-effect model, rather than treating it as statistical non-independence. So fitting a model like:

y = A + u

where A is the intercept and u is the covariance matrix based on phylogenetic relationships. Like a GAM where some non random noise is to be controlled for to better estimate the linear model. I think what I want is to just estimate y=A without the 'u', but accounting for the fact that each row in the data represents < 1 independent data point according to some known pattern of data point covariances (i.e. the phylogenetic covariance matrix).

I'll probably post another question focused on this.

Best, Richard.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Richard,

You are running

inla(phenotype ~1 + f(spN, model="generic2", ..., Cmatrix = AinvSM), ...)

which is Gaussian likelihood (the default)

p(phenotype|Intercept, u, sigma2e) ~ N(1Intercept + Zu, Isigma2e), so phenotype = 1 Intercept + Zu + e
p(a, A, sigma2a) ~ N(0, A sigma2a)
p(sigma2e) ~ ...
p(sigma2a) ~ ...

to match IDs between your phenotype data (spN) and precision matrix (AinvSM) its best to ensure that you code your full list of spN (internal nodes and tips) from 1:N so that precision matrix rows and columns refer to 1:N effects and then in the phenotype data you will only have those 1:N that are actually observed. I hope this makes sense. Say you have 5x5 precision matrix, so 1:N is 1:5. Then say that you have observations on 3, 4 and 5 (the tips), then your spN column in the phenotype data will only have 3, 4 and 5. You will then get estimates for all 5 effects, spN1, spN2, spN3, spN4 and spN5 - since they are all connected via the precision matrix.

Are you fitting the same model in MCMCglmm? I am not fully clear, but from your description it seems you are thinking about phenotype = 1 Interecept + u (so not Zu, and also no residual). Does this mean you have only a single record per each level of spN? If so, then indeed you won't have sufficient data structure to separate u and e (the "Zu + e" is just "u + e"). You can use control.family to fix sigma2e to a "numerical" zero then, but be careful that the theta in control.family is (see documentation).

gg
